title: Regulatory institutions: Governance needs implementation markets
desc: Proposes public outcomes with competing private compliance methods, while debating process, accountability, research access and market structure.

kps.k: The cluster shifts the AI governance debate from writing rules to building institutions capable of implementing them.
kps.d: Hadfield and Clark argue that conventional governance faces both a technical deficit in translating legal goals into operational controls and a democratic deficit when industry decides acceptable risks. Hadfield’s legal-infrastructure proposal adds frontier-model registries, agent identification and regulatory markets. These are institutional-design arguments, not demonstrated solutions. The NYSBA task force takes a more context-dependent position: regulators should choose detailed rules, principles or self-regulation according to sectors, rights and risks, rather than impose a universal model.

qs.q: First is a technical deficit: Legislatures and regulators face significant challenges in rap- idly translating conventional command-and-control legal requirements into technical re- quirements.
qs.a: Regulatory Markets: The Future of AI Governance · Regulators & courts · 2023

qs.q: Second is a democratic deficit: Overreliance on industry to provide technical standards fails to ensure that the many values-based decisions that must be made to shape AI development and deployment are made by democratically accountable public, not private, actors.
qs.a: Regulatory Markets: The Future of AI Governance · Regulators & courts · 2023

kps.k: Regulatory markets would combine publicly determined outcomes with competing private methods, while retaining substantial government oversight.
kps.d: Hadfield and Clark propose mandatory purchases from licensed nonprofit or for-profit regulators that translate public outcomes into technical requirements. Competition would aim to attract investment in regulatory technology, not merely reduce compliance costs. Existing demand for red teaming motivates an initial application but does not establish that the market model works. The authors acknowledge that client payment, concentration, collusion and switching costs could reward leniency. Their safeguards require outcome audits, credible licence withdrawal, competition protections, public technical expertise and sustained funding; credit-rating failures and inadequate FAA oversight of Boeing serve as cautionary analogies.

qs.q: Governments require targets to purchase regulatory services (entering into a regulatory contract with a private regulator) and directly regulate the market for regulatory services, ensuring it operates in the public interest.
qs.a: Regulatory Markets: The Future of AI Governance · Regulators & courts · 2023

qs.q: Specifically, we focus on the goal of building a regulatory market not merely to recruit the expertise or cost-efficiency of non-state intermediaries but, more importantly, to attract investment of human and financial capital into the design and development of true regulatory technologies that can keep pace with AI.
qs.a: Regulatory Markets: The Future of AI Governance · Regulators & courts · 2023

kps.k: The sources differ over whether oversight should prioritize demonstrated outcomes or development processes.
kps.d: Regulatory Markets criticizes procedural risk-management systems for failing to supply technical methods for measuring and mitigating harms. By contrast, AI Governance and the Verification Gap argues that computational limits, opacity and post-release adaptation make final-product assurance inadequate and justify process controls adapted from Quality by Design. It cites EU lifetime monitoring requirements and reported investor diligence as indications that developer attestations do not suffice, not as measured proof of computational intractability. This is a difference in emphasis rather than a direct rebuttal: both approaches require continuing oversight, but the supplied material does not establish how process compliance translates into reliable safety outcomes.

qs.q: SSOs are responding with proce- dural solutions for a risk-management system, not technical detail about how to measure and mitigate risks.
qs.a: Regulatory Markets: The Future of AI Governance · Regulators & courts · 2023

qs.q: As this paper argues, the formal intractability of auditing makes it exceedingly difficult for a regulator to gain sufficient assurance of a model's internal safety before it is deployed.
qs.a: AI Governance and the Verification Gap: A Framework for Law and Policy Under Computational Intractability · Academia · 2025

kps.k: Accountability requires access to models, identifiable responsible parties and protection for independent research.
kps.d: Hadfield proposes frontier-model registration to improve government visibility and expertise without requiring universal public disclosure. Agent registration and counterparty checks could make revocation an economic sanction, not a technical shutdown; registration alone would not confer adequate legal personhood or ensure compensation. A Safe Harbor for AI Evaluation and Red Teaming addresses a complementary access problem through fair pre-registration and appeals procedures protecting good-faith researchers from unjustified account suspension. Its authors distinguish those protections from earlier, deeper or subsidized access and acknowledge that safe harbors do not supply missing research resources.

kps.k: Market structure is both a regulatory target and a constraint on effective oversight.
kps.d: An Antimonopoly Approach argues that discernible hardware, cloud and model-layer structures justify preventive rules alongside case-by-case antitrust enforcement despite rapid technical change. It predicts that interoperability and limits on infrastructure bottlenecks could support downstream innovation and choice. Open models alone cannot remove hardware and cloud concentration, although the authors do not dismiss their competitive value. This complements the regulatory-market proposal’s dependence on sufficient scale and multiple independent providers: competition must be sustained through institutional design, not assumed. Claims that competition would improve privacy or reduce bias remain possibilities rather than established effects.

qs.q: The Advantages of Ex Ante Governance      Our analysis of the AI technology stack and its market structure— coupled with an assessment of current law—also suggests that ex ante governance solutions are essential tools and important complements to ex post antitrust enforcement on a case-by-case basis.
qs.a: An Antimonopoly Approach to Governing Artificial Intelligence · Academia · 2024

qs.q: If there are only two or three companies involved in developing a particular type of AI, it will be difficult to sustain a competitive market of regulators, each of which needs to regulate multiple entities and each of which needs to be at risk of losing market share to prompt continual investment in better regulatory technology.
qs.a: Regulatory Markets: The Future of AI Governance · Regulators & courts · 2023

kps.k: Cross-border coordination need not mean uniform regulation, but national authority alone may leave gaps.
kps.d: The NYSBA task force predicts that domestic regulation will often need international cooperation because AI crosses borders. Hadfield and Clark offer multijurisdictional licensing as one mechanism: private regulators could serve several countries while each government retains its own outcome requirements. They anticipate lower compliance burdens and greater market scale without requiring US–China agreement on technical standards. These remain conditional benefits; geopolitical lobbying, divergent institutional powers and widely available models continue to constrain enforcement.

qs.q: We  believe in local, state and federal regulation where appropriate, but also propose that local, state  and federal regulation is likely to prove inadequate without international and sometimes global  cooperation, because AI is a cross-border phenomenon rather than a local one.
qs.a: Report and Recommendations of the New York State Bar Association Task Force on Artificial Intelligence (April 2024) · Regulators & courts · 2024

qs.q: Multiple pri- vate regulators, ideally, are licensed by multiple governments, each implement- ing their own outcome requirements.
qs.a: Regulatory Markets: The Future of AI Governance · Regulators & courts · 2023

kps.k: Practical recommendations emphasize credible controls and enforcement, while liability and adoption effects remain uncertain.
kps.d: The Verification Gap paper proposes audit trails and fraud deterrence, presenting FTC Section 5 enforcement against unsupported safety claims as a possible route rather than settled law or the optimal regulatory arrangement. The AI Fact Sheet 2026 supports calibrated private risk management and reports a forecast that up to 20% of large enterprises could face lawsuits and fines over inadequate agent controls by 2030; this is not an observed rate. Its cited experiment suggests factfinders may penalize AI-enabled conduct, but does not establish a general liability rule or resolve provider–deployer responsibility. Alongside compliance costs, the Verification Gap paper identifies a possible market-enabling benefit: clearer rules could encourage downstream enterprise adoption. The practical case for stronger governance therefore combines legal reasoning, limited experimental evidence and forecasts, rather than demonstrated system-wide effects.

qs.q: The FTC could use its authority under Section 5 of the FTC Act, which prohibits unfair or deceptive practices, to argue that making unsubstantiated safety or trustworthiness claims without a robust, RMF-aligned audit trail constitutes a deceptive practice [176], [177], [178].
qs.a: AI Governance and the Verification Gap: A Framework for Law and Policy Under Computational Intractability · Academia · 2025

qs.q: AI forecasters predict that up to 20% of large  enterprises will see lawsuits and fines due to  inadequate AI agent controls by 2030.22 Today’s state  of AI governance makes that a likely reality (or worse)  unless we improve AI governance immediately.
qs.a: Artificial Intelligence Risk Management 2026 (AI Fact Sheet 2026) · Liability insurers · 2026

vlens.an: Within this curated professional voice, the sources agree that AI governance requires more than abstract rule-writing: regulation must be operationally capable, tailored to risks and sectors, backed by credible public oversight, and responsive to cross-border activity. They differ materially on whether competing private compliance providers should be central to that capacity. Hadfield and Clark build on the proposition with a concrete regulatory-market design in which governments set outcomes, licensed private regulators compete over implementation methods, and public authorities audit results and impose sanctions. The New York State Bar Association Task Force instead redirects toward a context-specific mix of detailed rules, principles-based regulation and self-regulation, supplemented by international cooperation; it does not endorse an implementation market as the preferred institutional model. Accordingly, the voice is mixed on the cluster’s specific claim that governance needs implementation markets, despite broad common ground on the need for stronger implementation institutions. These sources are a curated selection and do not establish how prevalent either view is among regulators, courts or professional bodies.

vlens.an: The professional-liability-insurer source aligns with the proposition’s diagnosis that AI governance requires stronger, operational risk controls. It points to evolving standards, properly calibrated private-sector risk management, emerging liability exposure and an urgent need to improve controls for AI agents. This supplies a risk-based rationale for better implementation capacity rather than merely additional rulemaking. However, it does not address the proposition’s defining institutional design: publicly determined outcomes implemented through a competitive market of licensed private regulators under government oversight. Nor does it assess that model’s accountability, competition, concentration or cross-border features. Internal variation lies mainly in the basis for urgency: the source combines policy analysis with a forecast of future lawsuits and fines and tentative experimental evidence of an “AI penalty,” while leaving provider–deployer liability allocation unresolved. Because these considerations support stronger governance generally but neither endorse nor reject regulatory implementation markets, the position is unclear rather than supportive or opposed.

vlens.an: Across this curated set of academia and research sources, the principal proposition is accepted and materially developed: effective AI governance requires operational institutions, not substantive rules alone. The common rationale is that opacity, adaptive systems, limited public technical capacity, restricted research access and concentrated infrastructure prevent conventional rulemaking or developer attestations from reliably producing accountability. The sources therefore add concrete but complementary mechanisms: frontier-model and agent registries plus competitive regulatory markets; process-based oversight, continuous monitoring, audit trails and enforcement; procedural safe harbors for independent evaluation and red teaming; and ex ante antimonopoly controls addressing infrastructure bottlenecks. Material variation concerns what implementation should prioritize. Hadfield focuses most directly on markets of licensed private regulators operating under public outcomes; the verification-gap paper emphasizes development processes because final-product assurance may be technically inadequate; the safe-harbor proposal concentrates on researcher access and fair procedures; and the antimonopoly account treats competitive market structure as a prerequisite and regulatory target. These approaches complement rather than uniformly endorse regulatory markets specifically. They also share important limitations: most claimed benefits are institutional proposals, legal arguments or predictions rather than demonstrated outcomes, and private implementation remains dependent on credible public oversight, enforcement, resources and sustained competition.

qs.q: This situation necessitates a shift in regulatory focus from exclusively evaluating the final product to scrutinizing the process that 20 created it [57], [137].
qs.a: AI Governance and the Verification Gap: A Framework for Law and Policy Under Computational Intractability · Academia · 2025

elens.an: Taken together, the curated sources in the generative-shock period build on the proposition that AI governance requires institutions capable of implementation, not rule-writing alone. Their common premise is that rapid, technically complex and cross-border AI development exposes limitations in conventional governance and requires durable implementation capacity, independent evaluation and proactive intervention. Material extensions include licensed markets for private regulatory services under public outcome-setting and enforcement; procedural safe harbors for independent evaluation and red teaming; and ex ante antimonopoly measures addressing infrastructure bottlenecks that could undermine both innovation and regulatory competition. There is important internal variation. Regulatory Markets most directly develops the proposed implementation-market model, while the safe-harbor and antimonopoly sources add complementary conditions for it to function: researcher access, public technical capacity, credible sanctions and sufficiently competitive underlying markets. By contrast, the NYSBA task force redirects away from privileging regulatory markets, recommending a context-dependent mix of detailed rules, principles-based governance, self-regulation and international cooperation. Across these records, the proposals are principally institutional-design arguments and predictions rather than demonstrated evidence that the recommended arrangements produce reliable outcomes.

elens.an: The 2025 source accepts the proposition’s shift from abstract rules toward implementable governance and materially extends it with process-based oversight, continuous monitoring, audit trails and enforcement mechanisms suited to opaque, adaptive systems. It connects these institutions to adoption at scale by arguing that regulatory uncertainty may deter downstream enterprises and that clearer frameworks may create operational confidence. This adoption effect is presented as a possibility, not a demonstrated causal finding. There is also material variation within the source: governance may enable adoption, but process controls can impose performance, development-time and compute costs. The source does not endorse competing private regulatory markets specifically; it offers a complementary implementation model centred on development processes and credible public enforcement. Because the evidence consists of one curated source, its position should not be treated as representative of 2025 commentary generally.

elens.an: The 2026 sources collectively build on the proposition, although they do so unevenly. Hadfield directly accepts and materially develops the institutional shift from substantive rules toward implementation capacity: she specifies frontier-model registration, agent identification and competitive regulatory markets in which private providers translate public outcomes into operational requirements. She also stresses that this arrangement depends on effective public oversight, careful market design and credible licensing sanctions; its benefits remain proposed rather than demonstrated. The AI Fact Sheet supports the broader need for stronger, promptly improved governance through emerging standards, liability concerns, a forecast of lawsuits and fines, and limited experimental evidence, but it neither endorses nor evaluates competing private regulatory providers. Thus, within this curated selection, the period’s clearest contribution is a concrete extension of the implementation-market model, accompanied by a more general risk-management case that reinforces urgency without resolving institutional design.
